title: The 'force' variant of a reset flow is reachable without a session and without a token
index_line: T-0046 · AUTH_DECISION · an administrative force-reset endpoint skips the token check the normal reset performs · java/dotnet/node · corroborated
invariant_violated: A password-reset flow is assumed to be safe because it is *the* flow that has to be reachable without a session, and it is guarded by a token instead. A second endpoint exists for administrators to force a reset without the user's involvement — it reasonably skips the token, and unreasonably also skips the caller's authentication, because 'only an admin can reach it' was assumed rather than enforced.

mechanism.does: an unauthenticated attacker posts to the administrative force-reset endpoint, naming the system administrator account
the API resolves the target account from the supplied identifier and selects the admin record
the endpoint performs none of the checks the normal reset performs — no reset token, no existing password, no caller session
the new password is written to the administrator account
the attacker authenticates as the administrator, and the product's own administrative features supply execution

sink.auth.jwt-verify.value: the token/credential verification call site that the *normal* reset path uses and this path omits — the absence is the bug

source.http.request.value: one anonymous POST naming the target account; no cookie, no token, no CSRF

guard.none.value: the assumption that the endpoint is unreachable except by an administrator, with no check that it is

oracle.error.value: the endpoint's response distinguishes 'account exists' from 'account does not', which makes target selection trivial

preconditions.expr: the reset API is reachable without a session
the force/administrative variant exists alongside the token-based flow and shares its account-write path
the normal reset path verifies a token while the force path does not — diff the two handlers

spec.method: compare the two controller methods: the difference in their guard clauses is the finding

success: an anonymous POST changes the administrator's password, and the attacker then logs in with it
the normal reset endpoint correctly demands a token — the asymmetry between the two endpoints is the proof
the endpoint's response leaks whether the target account exists
failure_like: the force endpoint requires a caller session with administrative rights
both variants funnel through one verification function that the force path cannot skip
false_positive: a 401 returned by the endpoint with no body — the endpoint is guarded; the finding needs the password to actually change
reset emails being sent: that is the token flow working, not a bypass

hazards: the audit unit is the *pair* of endpoints: any administrative variant of a user-facing flow is a candidate for a missing check
administrative endpoints are often excluded from authentication reviews because 'the UI only shows them to admins' — the UI is not the gate
after reset you have admin, and admin usually means the vendor's own execution features; impact is full compromise, not just account takeover
this is not the same as T-0035 (JIT provisioning trusts a claim): here no IdP is involved at all — the check is simply absent on one route
non_transfers: systems whose force-reset requires an authenticated admin session
designs where both variants call one guarded function
